transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-27 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~75 minutes
Attendees: Danielle Park (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Raj Patel (Aquila CTO), Elena Gomez (Aquila ML), Tom Wu (Aquila Infra)

[00:00] Danielle: hey everyone, thanks for joining. we're going to deep-dive into GPU runtime profiling — kernel selection, tenso r t-llm vs vLLM behavior, cuda graphs and kv cache stuff. maya and i will cover the runtime side, and then we'll go into profiling artifacts. quick round robin?
[00:18] Raj: hey, raj here, i'll be owning success criteria. main things for us are 95th p99 latency under 200ms for 2k token responses and consistent throughput at peak — about 120 concurrent reqs.
[00:30] Elena: elena — will drive the model perf tests and will provide the prompt sets. we've got a few finetuned llama2 variants and a 33B open model we want to evaluate.
[00:40] Tom: tom — infra. i care about VPC peering, egress, and how the KV cache interacts with our redis layer. also curious about on-prem install footprint.
[00:50] Maya: awesome. quick note — apologies for the audio earlier, i had my mic weird. we'll jump in.

[01:05] Maya: first slide, kernel selection. our runtime picks kernels based on model architecture, sequence length distribution, and device capabilities. we run a small micro-benchmark on model load to pick between attention kernels (flash attention variants) and matmul kernels. that decision often explains 10-30% perf delta.
[01:30] Elena: when you say small micro-bench, is that runtime-only or dataset-profiled? we have long prefix-heavy conversation logs, so average seq length is skewed.
[01:42] Maya: good call — we do both. by default the heuristic uses a short synthetic micro-bench (latency-focused) and then optionally an input distribution profile if you provide sample traces; that shifts kernels toward long-seq optimized paths.

[02:10] Raj: how deterministic is kernel selection between runs? in our trials with other runtimes we've seen oscillation and non-deterministic perf.
[02:20] Maya: it's deterministic per model/instance once the profile is set. if you change quantization or batch hints, we re-evaluate. we also persist kernel choices to avoid jitter. occasional manual override available.

[03:00] Danielle: next — tensor r t-llm vs vll m. we ran side-by-side on A100 80GB and 4080-class — results were interesting. vLLM had better short-request latency out-of-box because of aggressive batching and a simpler execution path; tenso r t-llm gave better throughput for long sequences after kernel tuning and with cudagraph warmup.
[03:30] Raj: numbers? rough p50/p95/p99?
[03:36] Maya: quick ballpark from our internal benchmarks on the 33B model: vLLM p50 ~ 12ms/token, p95 ~ 45ms/token, p99 ~ 80ms/token under 8-token chunking; TensorRT-LLM p50 ~ 9ms/token, p95 ~ 30ms/token, p99 ~ 60ms/token — but tenso r t needed a cudagraph warmup of about 200 tokens to hit peak. also quantized TensorRT runs improved throughput by ~1.8x with 4-bit.
[04:10] Elena: that's consistent with what we saw — warmup is a problem for interactive bots. users perceive lag for the first few tokens. any tricks?
[04:18] Maya: yes — prefix caching + pre-warming CUDA graphs. two approaches: (1) have a tiny warmup request path that executes a minimal prompt to prepare graphs and caches; (2) keep a hot pool of warm-instances that handled similar seq lengths. both add cost but reduce cold-token latency.

[05:00] Tom: how does KV cache behave with redis? can we offload to a remote KV store?
[05:08] Maya: KV cache is best kept on-device (GPU) when possible — that avoids PCIe round trips. remote KV (redis) adds centi- to deci-seconds and kills token latency if you have prefix-heavy inputs. we do support hybrid approaches: short-term KV in-GPU, and aged KV spilled to redis with async prefetch.
[05:35] Raj: any memory-quant tradeoffs? if we quantize weights, does KV cache size shrink?
[05:42] Maya: quantization affects model weight memory not the KV cache directly (KV cache stores key/value tensors per token). but total memory headroom increases with quantized weights so you can host larger batch sizes or longer KV windows on-device.

[06:10] Danielle: let's talk CUDA graphs — what we see is that cudagraphs eliminate some launch overheads and kernel scheduling jitter, but they are brittle to dynamic sequence length changes.
[06:24] Maya: exact. cudagraphs are great if your step pattern is fairly static (e.g., chunked generation). if you have wildly varying lengths per request, you either build many graphs (costly) or fall back to non-graph execution. we suggest a hybrid: generate graphs for the common chunk sizes (8/16/32) and fall back otherwise.
[06:45] Elena: how do we capture graphs in our environment? any sample code?
[06:50] Maya: yes — i'll drop the sample in the runbook. it shows how to capture, replay, and verify graphs. it also includes heuristics for graph caching and eviction based on hit rate.

[07:20] Raj: can you describe the profiling workflow? we want something repeatable and automatable.
[07:27] Maya: absolutely — start with a baseline micro-bench (single token, 1 thread), then run a full harness that simulates your concurrency and prefix distributions. we collect CUDA timeline traces, kernel occupancy, and NVTX regions. we also diff kernel choices between runs. the runbook includes a CI job that posts perf artifacts to a shared S3.

[08:10] Danielle: i want to flag a real-world case: one customer hit 2x p95 regression after switching to int8 quantization via a naive pipeline — caused by attention kernel fallback in mixed-precision paths.
[08:25] Elena: that scares me — does Redwood detect and avoid bad kernel combos?
[08:30] Maya: yes, our selector prefers kernels with validated numerical stability for a quantization profile. we run correctness checks on a small input set and will fall back or recommend 4-bit instead of 8-bit if we find regressions.

[09:05] Tom: for on-prem, what are the infra requirements and SSO/KMS integrations?
[09:13] Danielle: private deployment supports customer-managed control plane in your VPC and an on-prem package. we integrate with commonly used KMS/HSM and SAML-based SSO. our docs list required ports, driver versions, and docker/agent images.
[09:35] Tom: do you have HSM examples? our security team insists on HSM-backed keywraps.
[09:40] Danielle: yes — we have an HSM integration guide (AWS CloudHSM, Azure Dedicated HSM, and PKCS#11 examples) and a template for KMS key policies. we'll share that doc.

[10:20] Raj: penciling timeline — we want a pilot in Jan to validate latency and cost. what are blockers?
[10:28] Maya: blockers are: shared perf harness, network topology for VPC peering, and initial model artifacts. once those are in place we can provision a 2-node GPU cluster and run the benchmark suite in 2-3 days.

[11:00] [noise/crosstalk] Danielle: quick detour — batching strategies.
[11:05] Maya: batching increases throughput but can increase tail latency. we tune batching by a target-latency policy: optimal batch size is computed from observed seq length distribution and desired p95 target. we also support latency-first queues which cut batches when latency budget is hit.
[11:35] Elena: what about dynamic batching vs synthetic batching? which is better for fairness?
[11:40] Maya: dynamic batching is better for utilization; synthetic batching (padding to same length) can be simpler but wastes compute. for fair multi-tenant setups we recommend per-tenant rate-limiting and per-route batching knobs.

[12:10] Danielle: a note on monitoring — console shows token-level latency and percentiles, model route breakdown, and kernel-level counters so you can see if a kernel change impacted p95.
[12:25] Raj: will that expose kernel names? our ops team wants to correlate regressions to kernel swaps.
[12:30] Maya: yes — kernel id and version are part of the trace metadata.

[13:00] Elena: quantization specifics — what's supported? GPTQ, PTQ, 4-bit, 8-bit?
[13:08] Maya: we support PTQ and GPTQ-style recipes, 8-bit and 4-bit variants, and some mixed-precision paths in TensorRT-LLM. vLLM supports int8 for some ops but less aggressive 4-bit support. quality vs perf tradeoffs are documented per model.

[13:50] Raj: if we do 4-bit, do we risk more hallucinations or quality drops?
[13:56] Maya: potentially — we recommend automated evals that compare model output on your prompt set; the Optimize toolkit can run quality regressions and surface diffs. often 4-bit is acceptable for many tasks, but you should test.

[14:30] Tom: last infra Q — how do you handle kernel updates / driver updates on private? we have strict change windows.
[14:38] Maya: kernel and runtime updates are managed by your control plane. we provide image tags and upgrade playbooks; upgrades can be staged to canary nodes first. we also provide a compatibility matrix for CUDA, driver versions, and TensorRT versions.

[15:10] Danielle: quick recap and next steps. danielle to send pricing and runbook; maya to share cudagraph sample code and kernel selector logs; elena to share prompt set and SLOs; tom to provision VPC/test infra. schedule pilot kickoff for Jan week 2.
[15:30] Raj: sounds good. any objections?
[15:34] Elena: none. thanks all.

[15:45] Danielle: i'll follow up with meeting notes and links to artifacts (runbook, sample code, security docs).

[15:50] [meeting end]
